A slow attempt to write down the conceptual structure of spectroscopy — from
what a photon is to what a detector actually records — one question at a time.

Each page opens with a short answer that should be enough on its own. Longer
derivations sit below it in collapsible sections, so the page stays readable
whether you want the idea or the algebra.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## How to read this
Answers are written for someone with a physics background who has not
necessarily worked in many-body theory. Where a statement hides a subtlety, it
says so rather than smoothing it over. Corrections are welcome —
[email me](mailto:riccardo.reho@uni.lu).
:::

## Fields, photons, coherence

What the electromagnetic field is quantum mechanically, and in what sense a
laser beam is "classical".

::: {#l-fields}
:::

## Response and spectroscopy

Why nearly every spectroscopy, whatever the apparatus, ends up measuring the
same mathematical object.

::: {#l-response}
:::

## Green functions and the contour

The propagator, why it needs two time arguments out of equilibrium, and what
the contour is really doing.

::: {#l-green}
:::

## Self-energy and excitations

Where interaction effects live, and how a bound electron–hole pair shows up in
a measurable spectrum.

::: {#l-excitations}
:::

## From response to measurement

Closing the loop: induced currents, propagating light, and the number a
detector reports.

::: {#l-measurement}
:::
